chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Hafs ibn al-Bakhtari, from Mansur ibn Hazim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding the man whose sacrificial animal (hady) strays, so another man finds it and slaughters it, he (peace be upon him) said: 'If he had slaughtered it at Mina, it has sufficed for its owner from whom it had strayed; and if he had slaughtered it in other than Mina, it has not sufficed for its owner.'

key_terms.أَجْزَأَ: It sufficed / was valid (for the religious obligation)
key_terms.مِنًى: Mina, a sacred site near Mecca where specific Hajj rituals occur
key_terms.هَدْيُ: Sacrificial animal (camel, cow, or sheep) offered during Hajj or Umrah

ai.seo_question: Does a found stray sacrificial animal count for the owner if slaughtered outside Mina?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi clarifies the geographical validity of the Hady sacrifice, emphasizing that the ritual's efficacy is tied to the specific sanctity of Mina, a key pillar of Hajj rites. It reflects the Shia juristic view that the location of slaughter is a condition for the acceptance of the offering, distinguishing between the sacred precincts and other areas. This ruling ensures that the spiritual intent of the sacrifice remains aligned with the Prophet's practice during the Farewell Pilgrimage.
